analysis.one_liner: Eases and speeds black lung benefit claims for sick coal miners and their survivors.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate HELP Committee the day it was introduced, never received a committee vote, and died when the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: Coal miners who develop black lung disease from breathing coal dust can claim federal disability benefits, but claims involve complex, adversarial litigation against mine operators. This bill would have made it easier to win a claim: it set stricter medical presumptions that favor miners, required mine operators to hand over all medical evidence they develop, had the government pay miners' attorney fees and medical expenses, paid for full lung evaluations and CT scans, authorized reopening claims denied on the basis of x-rays later deemed unreliable, and restored cost-of-living increases to benefits. Liable mine operators would repay the fund for those expenses.
analysis.who_benefits: Coal miners disabled by black lung disease, and surviving spouses, children, and dependent family members of deceased miners. Also black lung clinics and claimant-side attorneys, whose services would be funded through the program.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Sick coal miners and their survivors

how_it_helps.text: Creates an irrebuttable presumption of total disability when complicated pneumoconiosis (large lung lesions over 1 cm) is established by x-ray, biopsy, or autopsy, and a rebuttable presumption for miners with 15+ years in the mines whose impairment is documented [S3].

Requires every party, including mine operators, to disclose all medical information developed about the miner's condition even if they do not intend to use it as evidence; the bill's findings record that some operators' representatives withheld evidence that would have supported miners' claims [S3].

Establishes a program, paid from the Black Lung fund and reimbursed by liable operators, to pay up to $4,500 in attorney fees and $3,000 in medical expenses per contested claim not resolved within a year; the bill's findings note only 33 percent of claimants have an attorney at the initial determination [S3].

Requires the Labor Department to provide claimants, on request, a complete pulmonary evaluation with a conflict-screened physician, authorize CT scans for diagnosing complicated pneumoconiosis, and pay the costs from the fund [S3].

Lets claimants whose cases were denied on x-ray readings by a physician the Labor Department later deemed not credible file a new claim within one year, with benefits backdated to the original denial [S3].

Restores automatic cost-of-living increases tied to a wage index rather than the federal pay rate that had been frozen, resolving doubt in the claimant's favor when evidence is evenly balanced, and letting clinics use federal funds to help miners file claims [S3].
Directs retrospective studies of continuous dust monitor data to determine whether respirable dust limits should be tightened further to protect miner health [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Coal mine operators and their insurers, who would reimburse the federal fund for attorney fees and medical expenses on claims they lose, face mandatory disclosure of all medical evidence, stricter presumptions of disability, and possible sanctions, disqualification of attorneys and expert witnesses, and revised dust standards.
analysis.who_pays_short: Coal mine operators and their insurers

drawbacks.text: The cost would fall on mine operators and their insurers, and on the Black Lung Disability Trust Fund in cases where no liable operator can pay; higher benefits, fund-paid evaluations, and expanded presumptions all increase draw on a fund financed by coal excise taxes [S3].

The irrebuttable presumption for complicated pneumoconiosis and the automatic 2015 benefit increase are fixed rules that remove case-by-case judgment and could raise benefit costs regardless of individual circumstances [S3].
Mandatory disclosure of all medical evidence runs in both directions, so miners and their doctors would also have to turn over information they might prefer to keep out of the record [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For sick miners the bill removes the main structural disadvantages the bill's own findings describe: resource gaps against well-funded operators, withheld medical evidence, unreliable x-ray readings, and multi-year delays averaging nearly two years. The cost is higher benefit and litigation expenses concentrated on coal operators and the trust fund. The tradeoff is deliberate and the bill states its reasoning plainly; the design concern is the size of the added draw on the trust fund, not fairness of the process changes.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee on the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Robert Casey of Pennsylvania introduced the bill on April 5, 2017, with Senators Brown, Manchin, Kaine, and Warner as original cosponsors [S1].
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions [S5].
No further action was ever taken: no hearings, markup, committee vote, or floor vote appears in the bill's action history for the remainder of the 115th Congress [S5].
The bill had four cosponsors, all Democrats, in addition to its Democratic sponsor [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Coal mine operators and their insurers are better off because the bill died: they would have borne higher benefit costs, mandatory disclosure of medical evidence they currently can withhold, stricter disability presumptions, and reimbursement of miners' fees. Miners whose claims were denied under discredited x-ray readings remained denied.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Coal mine operators and their insurers

for.name: Sen. Robert Casey (D-PA)
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Black Lung Benefits Improvement Act of 2017 on April 5, 2017.

for.name: Sens. Sherrod Brown (D-OH), Joe Manchin (D-WV), Tim Kaine (D-VA), and Mark Warner (D-VA)
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction; no further recorded action.

against.name: Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral on April 5, 2017 and took no action on it for the rest of the 115th Congress; no hearing, markup, or committee vote is recorded.

sides.party_line_note: All five sponsors were Democrats from coal-mining states; no Republican cosponsor signed on, and the Republican-led HELP Committee took no action.

industries.industry: Coal mine operators and their insurers
industries.note: The bill shifts claim costs onto them: liable operators must reimburse the fund for miners' attorney fees and medical expenses, disclose all medical evidence, face stricter disability presumptions and discovery sanctions, and may see dust standards tightened. Their gain from the status quo is contested claims resolved in their favor.

industries.industry: Physicians and law firms retained by operators to contest claims
industries.note: The bill's findings record that some certified B Readers systematically misclassified miners' chest x-rays while working for coal operators, and that the Labor Department stopped crediting one widely used physician's negative readings; the bill creates conflict-of-interest screening, disqualification of attorneys and expert witnesses who misrepresent, and a panel program for impartial x-ray classifications.

industries.industry: Black lung clinics and claimant-side attorneys
industries.note: Clinics may use federal funds to help miners file claims, and a new program pays up to $4,500 in attorney fees and $3,000 in documented medical expenses on qualifying claims, expanding paid work for claimant representation.
